title: The Fox and the Cock
intro: A fox puts on a preacher’s dress and sends for the cock to call the faithful to dawn prayer. For a bird whose crow already marks first light, the invitation seems beautifully chosen. The cock has a family tradition of his own to set against the sermon. His ancestors had good reason to know this particular preacher.

translation: One day the fox stepped out
in the garb of those who preach.
1.sharh: A change of costume is enough to give the fox an audience. The opening verb makes his first appearance almost a public entrance.

translation: He went about the earth spouting words
and railing at the crafty.
2.sharh: The narrator supplies a judgement in the verb for babbling. The fox, meanwhile, wins an air of honesty by choosing the very vice for which his species is proverbial.

translation: “Praise be to God,” he said,
“the God of all the worlds.
3.sharh: The phrase recalls the opening praise of the Qur’an. A listener can recognise the devotional cadence at once, long before learning what the speaker wants.

translation: Servants of God, repent.
He is a refuge for those who turn back.
4.sharh: “Refuge” is the word in this performance. The printed “cave” gives physical shape to the shelter promised to anyone who repents.

translation: Renounce the birds. The life worth living
is the life of those who go without.
5.sharh: The sermon becomes unexpectedly specific about food. Renouncing birds does double service as pious advice and as reassurance for the guest the fox has in mind.

translation: Send for the cock to give the call
for our dawn prayer.”
6.sharh: A cock really does announce the dawn. Turning that familiar sound into the call to prayer gives the errand a plausibility the fox could never achieve by simply inviting him to breakfast.

translation: A messenger came to the cock
from the leader of the devout.
7.sharh: The messenger lends the invitation a degree of ceremony. In the space of a few lines the preacher in borrowed clothes has become head of a religious community.

translation: He laid the matter before him,
hoping the cock would yield.
8.sharh: “Yield” lets us feel the pressure behind an invitation presented as an honour. The messenger has to wait while the bird composes his answer.

translation: “Excuse me,” the cock replied,
“most misguided of the rightly guided.
9.sharh: The polite opening is followed by an impossible superlative. The messenger who believes in this spiritual guide has lost his way rather badly.

translation: Carry this from me to the fox,
on the word of my righteous forebears,
10.sharh: The messenger can carry a reply as easily as an invitation. The cock gives his answer a chain of family authorities and borrows the preacher’s religious vocabulary for them.

translation: those wearers of crowns
who entered that accursed belly.
11.sharh: The crowns are the combs on the cocks’ heads. The location of these august authorities gives their testimony an intimacy no court of inquiry could improve on.

translation: They used to say, and the best words
are the words of those who know,
12.sharh: The cock can afford a little solemnity now. “Those who know” has acquired a grimly precise meaning since the preceding line.

translation: ‘Whoever once supposed
a fox had faith was wrong.’”
13.sharh: The reply finally names the fox and the quality his performance was meant to prove. A judgement won at the cost of several generations outweighs the sermon.

1.1.1.meaning: Appeared in public, as someone about to put on a performance.

1.2.2.head: شِعار
1.2.2.meaning: Garb or distinguishing dress by which a group can be recognised.

1.2.3.head: واعِظ
1.2.3.meaning: A preacher who offers moral or religious admonition. The line sustains the plural ending in rhyme.

2.1.4.head: هَذى
2.1.4.meaning: Babbled, spoke at length without making sound sense.

2.2.2.head: ماكِر
2.2.2.meaning: A schemer who conceals what he is trying to achieve.

3.2.3.head: العالَمين
3.2.3.meaning: All worlds or all creation, a familiar expression of praise.

4.2.2.meaning: A refuge. Al-Waaedh calls God a shelter for those who repent. Shawqi’s first edition and both later printings have kahf, a cave.

5.1.1.head: اِزهَدوا
5.1.1.meaning: Renounce, willingly give up a thing one could otherwise enjoy.

5.2.3.head: زاهِد
5.2.3.meaning: An ascetic, one who forgoes worldly comforts as a religious discipline.

6.1.3.head: أَذَّنَ
6.1.3.meaning: Gave the call that announces the time for prayer.

6.2.1-2.head: صَلاة الصُّبح
6.2.1-2.meaning: The dawn prayer. A cock crows at daybreak, which gives the fox a plausible reason to send for him.

7.2.2.head: إِمام
7.2.2.meaning: A leader followed in religious practice, the office the messenger attributes to the fox.

7.2.3.head: ناسِك
7.2.3.meaning: A religious devotee. The fox has acquired a whole following in the wording of the message.

8.2.4.head: لانَ
8.2.4.meaning: Yielded or relented in the face of persuasion.

9.1.3.head: عُذر
9.1.3.meaning: “Pardon me”, a courteous introduction to a refusal.

9.2.2-3.head: أَضَلّ المُهتَدين
9.2.2-3.meaning: “Most astray of those rightly guided”, a pointed form of address to the emissary.

10.1.1.head: بَلِّغ
10.1.1.meaning: Deliver or pass on a message in the speaker’s name.

10.2.1-2.meaning: “On the authority of my forebears”. The cock names his chain of witnesses before telling what happened to them.

11.1.2-3.head: ذَوو التّيجان
11.1.2-3.meaning: “Wearers of crowns”, the dead cocks with their bright upright combs.

11.2.3.head: اللَّعين
11.2.3.meaning: Accursed, applied to the belly that swallowed the birds.

12.2.3.head: عارِف
12.2.3.meaning: One who knows by experience. These witnesses encountered the fox at first hand.

13.2.3.head: دين
13.2.3.meaning: Faith as a moral restraint, what would bind a preacher to his own words.
